analysis.one_liner: Requires websites to get permission-style notice before collecting or selling personal data, enforced by the FTC.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill to protect online privacy got two committee hearings over two years but never came up for a vote, and it died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required commercial websites and online services to tell visitors what personal information they collect, how they use it, and what gets shared with other companies, and to give people a way to limit or opt out of that sharing. The Federal Trade Commission would write and enforce the rules, with state attorneys general able to sue violators on behalf of residents. The committee that received the bill held hearings but never voted to send it to the Senate floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary internet users. Anyone who gave a website their name, address, email, phone number, or Social Security number would get clear notice of what is being collected, a simple process to limit disclosure of their information, the right to ask what data was sold to other companies and get a copy of it, and protection through required security procedures [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Websites would have to post a clear notice stating who operates the site, what personal information is collected, how it is used, and what may be shared with other companies [S3].

Users would get a simple online process to consent to or limit disclosure of their personal information for purposes beyond what they signed up for, and could request a description of any of their data sold or transferred to outside companies and a means to obtain that data [S2][S3].

Operators would have to maintain reasonable procedures to protect the confidentiality, security, and integrity of personal information, and the FTC would enforce violations as unfair or deceptive practices, with state attorneys general empowered to sue on behalf of residents [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Commercial websites, online services, advertisers, and data brokers would bear the cost of compliance: building notice and opt-out systems, honoring access requests, securing data, and giving up the unrestricted ability to collect and sell customer information [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Web operators, advertisers, and data brokers

drawbacks.text: The bill requires an opt-out, not an opt-in: companies could keep collecting and selling data until a user affirmatively objects, a weaker standard than privacy advocates sought [S3].

Industry-written self-regulatory guidelines, once approved by the FTC, would count as full compliance under a 'safe harbor,' letting marketing and online industries effectively set their own rules [S3].

Large carve-outs exist: companies would not have to offer purpose limits for transactional data or 'legitimate business activity,' could deny access to commercially confidential data from outside sources, and could even terminate the service of users who refuse to let their data be kept [S3].
The bill preempts state privacy laws that conflict with it, and enforcement runs only through the FTC and state attorneys general, so individuals could not sue on their own behalf [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary people, the bill offered real but modest protection: meaningful notice, some control over sharing, and access to sold data, at the price of compliance costs for online businesses that critics of the era argued could chill small e-commerce. Its biggest weaknesses were the opt-out rather than opt-in default, the self-regulation safe harbor, and the broad business-purpose exemptions, which would have left much data collection untouched. Even so, it would have created the first federal baseline for adult online privacy; nothing comparable existed.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, got two hearings, and was never voted out of committee before the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Senator Conrad Burns, a Republican, introduced the bill with Senator Ron Wyden in April 1999, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S3][S5].
The committee's Communications Subcommittee held a hearing in July 1999, and the full committee held another hearing in October 2000 [S5].
The bill was never reported out of committee and never received a vote in the Senate before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Online companies, advertisers, and data brokers kept collecting and selling personal information with no federal baseline of notice, opt-out, or access rights, and the country went without a comprehensive adult online privacy law. Congress itself was unaffected. Better off because the bill died: web operators and data brokers who faced compliance costs and limits on their data business.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican senator sponsored the bill with a Democratic co-introducer and two Democratic cosponsors; there was no floor vote, so no party split on passage can be measured [S3][S4][S5].

industries.note: Their business depends on collecting, sharing, and selling personal information, which the bill would have restricted with notice, opt-out, access, and security requirements. Users would have gained visibility into what data was sold about them [S3].

The bill would have imposed compliance costs on every commercial site collecting personal information, though the self-regulation safe harbor would have let many satisfy the rules through FTC-approved industry guidelines [S3].

The bill would have made FTC-approved guidelines written by representatives of the marketing and online industries a substitute for compliance with federal regulations, formalizing industry self-regulation as a permanent channel [S3].
